title: Verification · Economics
description: Connect claims to discriminating evidence on the final code state, challenge shared assumptions and account for the whole cost of producing accepted work.

sections.title: A green result is an answer to a particular question

blocks.body:
The retry patch arrives with a reassuring message: “All checks passed.” Imagine opening the log and discovering that the checks were a formatter and a linter. The message might be literally true, yet it says almost nothing about whether two retries now permit three attempts. The problem is the distance between what was measured and what the reader is invited to believe.

Verification begins by closing that distance. Take one claim: under repeated timeouts, the helper stops after three calls when given two retries. We need an observation that could differ if the claim were false. A test that counts calls under repeated timeouts can provide one. Formatting cannot, because both the correct and incorrect loops may be equally well formatted.

Other claims require other observations. Checking that the first timeout object reaches the caller requires distinguishable error objects and an assertion about identity. Checking that a non-timeout error stops the loop requires a trace containing that error. Inspecting the signature can show that its shape is unchanged; it cannot by itself show that callers still receive compatible behaviour.

It helps to imagine every claim with a line leading to its evidence. Some lines lead to a test result, others to an inspected diff or a reproduced interaction. If a line ends at the agent's own sentence restating the claim, we have not reached an observation yet. If it leads to a test, ask what that test actually exercises.

This is different from the evaluation question in chapter five. Evaluation asks how the workflow behaves across a sample of tasks. Verification asks what supports acceptance of this result. A good evaluation depends on meaningful verification; a carefully verified patch still does not establish that the workflow will succeed on every task.

data.title: Evidence must distinguish the claim
data.caption: Both implementations may satisfy the formatter. A check that observes call count can separate the intended behaviour from the extra-attempt mistake.

sections.title: Could the check notice the mistake?

blocks.body:
Return to the three-timeout trace. Suppose the new test passes on the patch. Now run that same test against the old implementation, in an isolated checkout. If the old implementation has the reported extra-attempt bug, we expect the test to fail for that reason. Seeing the relevant failure gives us evidence that the test distinguishes the defect we meant to repair.

If it also passes on the old implementation, investigate before celebrating. Perhaps the test imports a generated copy, the mock never reaches the loop, or the chosen input does not exercise the boundary. It is also possible that the old implementation never had the suspected bug. The test result is telling us that our story and our experiment do not yet line up.

Sometimes the original defect is inconvenient to reconstruct. We can still ask whether a check detects a deliberately introduced nearby error. Temporarily allow one extra call, or return the last timeout instead of the first. Does the relevant check fail? Make that experiment in a disposable copy and retain the real patch unchanged. The general technique of introducing small code changes to assess tests is called [mutation testing](https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/).

A surviving change is a question, not an automatic verdict against the test suite. The change might preserve behaviour for all relevant inputs, or it might expose a genuine gap. A detected change establishes sensitivity to that particular mistake. It does not prove complete correctness. We gain useful confidence by choosing alternatives that are plausible and consequential for this task.

For our helper, the alternatives almost choose themselves: one too many attempts, no initial call when retries are zero, a swallowed terminal error, the wrong timeout object, an extra wait after exhaustion. These are different claims about observable traces. Covering the loop's lines is not the same as distinguishing those behaviours.

blocks.question: The regression test passes on both the original code and the proposed fix. Is the fix necessarily wrong?
blocks.answer: No. The check may miss the defect, execute the wrong code, or reveal that the original diagnosis was wrong. It has not demonstrated that the proposed change fixes the reported behaviour. Investigate what the test executes and which observation should differ.

sections.title: When the patch and the test agree about the wrong thing

blocks.body:
There is a subtle trap in asking the same agent to write both the patch and its tests. Suppose it interprets two retries as two total attempts. It can produce an implementation that makes two calls and a test that expects two calls. Everything agrees. The disagreement is with the contract outside that little world.

Having a second agent read the patch may help, but a second opinion can inherit the same ambiguous wording. Independence is most valuable when it introduces a different basis for judgement. Read the established API contract. Trace an existing caller that relies on an initial call plus retries. Derive the expected sequence before examining the implementation. Each route creates an opportunity for the shared mistake to become visible.

The same applies to generated tests that mirror internal code. If a test recomputes the expected count with the same expression as the loop, it can reproduce the same off-by-one error. A small explicit trace may provide stronger evidence because its expected result comes from the contract rather than from a copy of the implementation.

Not all important properties fit into unit tests. Scope needs a diff review. An externally visible behaviour may need an integration check. A generated artefact may need inspection after the build. The verification effort should follow what could make this change unacceptable, rather than accumulating unrelated green commands.

That also limits unnecessary work. If a small local edit has relevant checks and there is no unresolved concern, endlessly rerunning unrelated suites adds little evidence. If a check reveals a new boundary—perhaps the caller translates timeout errors—then broadening the investigation has a reason. Each additional check should answer a question that matters to acceptance.

sections.title: Evidence belongs to the state that produced it

blocks.body:
Even an excellent test can be attached to the wrong patch. Imagine the agent runs the retry suite, sees it pass, then makes one last cleanup edit. The final message cites the earlier result. That result belongs to the earlier state. Whether it still supports the final patch depends on what changed, and a behaviour-affecting edit needs the relevant checks again.

Record enough identity to reconnect the evidence to the work: the tested revision, any uncommitted changes, the command, the working directory and the relevant environment. A commit identifier alone is insufficient when the test ran against a dirty working tree. A green exit code alone is insufficient when the runner skipped the suite or selected another package.

This does not require burying a reviewer under every log line. A useful handoff can be compact: the behaviour changed, the cases exercised on the final state, and the remaining limitation. The supporting output should be retrievable if the reviewer needs to challenge the conclusion.

Suppose the unit traces pass but the integration service is unavailable. “Local attempt and error behaviour verified; integration compatibility untested because the service could not be reached” gives a reviewer something actionable. It neither discards the evidence that exists nor invents the evidence that is missing. Depending on the task's acceptance boundary, the patch may be ready for review, ready for a later integration check, or not yet acceptable.

We can now make the evaluation's acceptance decision more meaningful. But an accepted result can still be expensive to obtain. The final part of the loop asks what all this work consumed.

sections.title: Put the unfinished work back into the bill

blocks.body:
Consider ten attempted repair tasks. The model and tools consume thirty currency units. People spend ninety active minutes reviewing and repairing the outputs. For this fictional calculation, value that time at sixty units per hour, so it contributes another ninety units. Six results meet the acceptance rule by the end of the observation period.

The batch has consumed 120 units and produced six accepted results. Its observed cost per accepted result is 120 divided by six: twenty units. Dividing by ten gives twelve units per attempted task, which answers a different question. The resources spent on the four unaccepted tasks remain in the bill even though their results do not enter the accepted count.

The arithmetic can be written as:

$$C = \frac{M + H + O}{A}$$

Here, C is cost per accepted result, M is machine cost, H is active human cost, O is allocated operating cost, and A is the number of accepted results. Express the three costs in the same currency and use the same observation period throughout.

Our first calculation set the last term to zero for simplicity. In an operating system, setup, benchmark maintenance, environment repair and incident handling also consume resources. Decide how to allocate them over a stated period or workload. If no result is accepted, there is no finite observed cost per accepted result; reporting zero would reverse the meaning of the experiment.

Now compare a second workflow on the same ten tasks. Suppose it spends fifty units on tools but needs only forty active human minutes and gets seven results accepted. At the same hourly valuation, its measured total is ninety units, or about 12.86 per accepted result before allocated overhead. Its larger tool bill accompanies a lower total cost per accepted result. These fictional numbers show why optimising the visible API bill alone can choose the wrong workflow.

Acceptance quality and task mix must remain comparable. Cheaply accepting weaker patches would make the ratio improve while the engineering result deteriorates. Nor does this ratio erase the unfinished tasks: if all ten must eventually be completed, include the subsequent human fallback work in an end-to-end comparison. The cost of the agent's accepted outputs and the cost of completing the whole workload are related, but distinct measurements.

blocks.question: Four tasks remain unfinished in the ten-task batch. Can twenty units per accepted result be reported as the cost of completing all ten?
blocks.answer: No. That ratio describes the six accepted outputs and includes resources already spent on failures. To estimate the cost of completing all ten, also account for the remaining recovery or human fallback work and its outcomes.

sections.title: A useful average is the beginning of a decision

blocks.body:
Elapsed time adds another dimension. An unattended hour is not an hour of active labour, but a delayed result may still block someone else. Conversely, reducing active review time can free capacity without reducing payroll. State which benefit matters: lower spend, shorter waiting, more completed work, or more attention available for difficult tasks. Compare it with a credible alternative for the same work.

Then look behind the average. One difficult repair can dominate review time. A rare escaped defect may be absent from a small pilot while still mattering greatly to the decision. A sample with no such incident cannot establish that the risk is zero. This is a reason to keep task categories and failure costs visible, and to choose an initial operating boundary that the evidence can support.

You can bring these chapters together with a small investigation. Reconstruct a few tasks, define what acceptance means, and run a workflow under recorded conditions. For one apparently successful result, follow each important claim back to its evidence. For one costly or unsuccessful result, follow the human effort and attempted recoveries forward into the total. Compare with the current way the work gets done, marking estimated baseline figures as estimates.

The conclusion might be that routine local repairs are useful with review, while cross-service changes still consume too much investigation time. It might be that a better test command would do more than a different model. It might simply be that the sample is too small and a particular failure deserves another trial. Each is a useful result if the evidence explains it.

We now have a basis for choosing a system: a workload, observable acceptance conditions, a way to test claims and an account of the effort involved. The next chapter uses that basis to examine the available models, harnesses and environments. The question becomes which combination helps this work reach an acceptable result under the conditions we actually have.

data.title: Lab 4 · Follow the evidence and the effort
data.brief: Use a few real or reconstructed tasks to explore where acceptance and cost come from. Treat the small sample as an investigation, not a universal ranking.
steps: Choose three to five tasks and define the expected outcome before running them. Preserve their starting states and available evidence.
Record every task and attempt, including intervention, unresolved work and justified escalation.
For an apparently successful result, test whether its important claims are supported on the delivered state.
Account for machine usage and active human effort. Compare with the current workflow, labelling estimates and omitted costs.
Propose a bounded operating decision or a further experiment that follows from the findings.
deliverables: Task records with acceptance evidence and unresolved limitations
An effort and cost comparison with its assumptions
A decision justified by the observed cases
data.review: A useful conclusion explains the evidence behind acceptance, keeps failures in the accounting and stays within what this sample can establish. It need not find a saving or manufacture a failure.

practiceTemplates.title: Cost per accepted engineering result
practiceTemplates.prompt: A fictional batch costs {{machine}} currency units in machine usage and {{minutes}} active human minutes at 60 units/hour. It yields {{accepted}} accepted results. Find total cost per accepted result, including all attempted work.
practiceTemplates.hint: At 60 units/hour, each active minute costs one unit. Add machine and labour costs, then divide by accepted outcomes.
practiceTemplates.solution: ({{machine}} + {{minutes}}) / {{accepted}} = {{answer}} units/result. Keep elapsed waiting separate from active labour.

heading: What would make this result worth accepting?
lead: Trace a reassuring claim back to an observation that could contradict it. Then follow the effort all the way to acceptance to find out what the result actually cost.
outcomes: Choose checks that distinguish the intended result from plausible mistakes.
Recognise shared assumptions and evidence that belongs to a different code state.
Compare whole-workflow cost and value while retaining unfinished work and uncertainty.
